title: India's Quiet Energy Revolution: Domestic Coal Replaces Imports While Renewables Hit Record 17.9% of Generation
excerpt: Power plants designed for imported coal now run on over 50% domestic fuel as solar and wind electricity surges 29% year-on-year, reshaping the country's energy mix
body:
Two parallel shifts in India's energy sector are quietly redrawing the country's power landscape. Imported coal-based power plants — long dependent on fuel from Indonesia, South Africa, and Russia — are now running on more than 50 percent domestic coal, while renewable electricity generation hit a record 17.9 percent of total generation in May, up 29.3 percent year-on-year. Together, these trends mark the most significant restructuring of India's energy supply chain in years.

## The Coal Switch

India's 18.7 gigawatts of power plant capacity designed to run on imported coal have historically relied on higher-grade fuel from overseas, with Indonesian and South African coal forming the backbone of supply. These plants were engineered for lower-ash, higher-calorific-value coal that India's domestic mines do not naturally produce at the same grade.

That is changing. According to Reuters, 5.7 GW of that capacity is already operating on domestic coal this year, with trials underway to extend the switch to another 4.3 GW. Some facilities are now using as much as 70 percent local fuel, a figure that would have seemed implausible even two years ago.

The transformation has been enabled by plant operators gradually modifying their boilers and fuel-handling systems to process Indian coal, which carries higher ash content and lower energy density than typical imports. The coal ministry has sweetened the deal by offering "doorstep supply" to imported coal-based plants — essentially guaranteeing the quality and quantity of domestic fuel delivered to their sites.

Imported coal-based plants have already booked 16 million metric tons of domestic coal for their needs, according to government officials cited by Reuters, who could not be named as they are not authorised to speak to the media.



> **"The coal ministry has sweetened the deal by offering "doorstep supply" to imported coal-based plants — essentially guaranteeing the quality and quantity of domestic fuel delivered to their sites."**


The impact on import volumes is stark. Data from Indian coal trader iEnergy Natural Resources shows that coal imports from Indonesia fell approximately 21 percent in the January-to-April period compared to the same window last year, while imports from South Africa plummeted by 68 percent.

## A Government Target Exceeded

The shift exceeds the government's own ambitious targets. Earlier this year, officials told Reuters that India aimed to cut power sector coal imports by at least 30 percent — roughly 15 million tons — by asking plants to test increased blending with domestic coal. The 50-percent-plus domestic usage at some plants suggests the programme is running ahead of schedule.

The government had long sought to reduce coal imports for the power sector, but previous attempts faltered because imported-coal plants simply could not handle lower-quality domestic fuel without expensive modifications. What changed was a combination of policy pressure, improved domestic coal supply logistics, and — perhaps most significantly — the economics. The Iran war drove up global energy prices and made imported coal significantly more expensive, giving plant operators a strong financial incentive to accelerate the switch.

## Renewables Fill the Gap

The other half of the equation is equally important. Higher power generation from renewable sources — solar, wind, and small hydro — is freeing up domestic coal supplies, creating room for local fuel to be diverted to coastal plants that were previously import-dependent.

India's renewable electricity generation rose 29.3 percent in May compared to the same month last year, reaching a record 17.9 percent of the country's total electricity generation. The figure is notable not just for its growth rate but for the structural milestone it represents: nearly one-fifth of India's electricity is now coming from clean sources, up from single digits just a few years ago.

The surge is underpinned by India's aggressive solar and wind capacity additions, which have accelerated under the National Solar Mission and various state-level policies. India still relies on coal for approximately three-quarters of its electricity generation, but the renewable share is rising fast enough to materially affect the coal supply-demand balance.

## Broader Implications

The twin trends — coal import substitution and renewable growth — carry significant macroeconomic implications. India is the world's second-largest importer of thermal coal, and every million tons of imported coal replaced by domestic supply reduces the current account deficit and eases pressure on the rupee. In a year when global energy prices have been volatile due to the Iran conflict, this insulation from import price shocks is particularly valuable.

For the Indian diaspora, the energy transition has both direct and indirect significance. NRIs with investments in Indian power companies — Tata Power, Adani Green Energy, NTPC — are watching these structural shifts closely, as the competitive landscape between thermal and renewable generators continues to evolve. More broadly, reduced energy import dependence strengthens the Indian economy's resilience to global shocks, which in turn protects the purchasing power of the remittances that millions of NRI families send home.

India's path to its 2070 net-zero target remains long, and coal will dominate the energy mix for decades to come. But the combination of import substitution and record renewable generation suggests the transition is no longer a distant aspiration — it is underway, driven by both policy and economics, and accelerated by the geopolitical turbulence that has defined 2026.
